**Daniel Joshua Drucker** (born 23 June 1956)[[1]](#cite_note-whoswho-1) is a Canadian endocrinologist renowned for his breakthrough discoveries of the biological actions of glucagon-like peptides GLP-1 and GLP-2, including GLP-1's key role in stimulating glucose-dependent insulin secretion,[[3]](#cite_note-:0-3) reducing food intake,[[4]](#cite_note-:1-4) protecting the heart,[[5]](#cite_note-:2-5) and reducing systemic inflammation.[[6]](#cite_note-:3-6) His scientific research has been a driving force in GLP-1's journey from a newly discovered peptide sequence to the mechanism behind globally used and life-changing [therapeutics for type 2 diabetes and obesity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GLP-1_receptor_agonist "GLP-1 receptor agonist"). It has also driven transformative [new therapeutics for intestinal failure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teduglutide "Teduglutide") and other metabolic disorders.[[7]](#cite_note-7) A [Fellow of the Royal Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fellow_of_the_Royal_Society "Fellow of the Royal Society"),[[8]](#cite_note-royal-8) and laureate of the 2023 [Wolf Prize in Medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolf_Prize_in_Medicine "Wolf Prize in Medicine"), he is a University Professor of [Medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Toronto_Faculty_of_Medicine "University of Toronto Faculty of Medicine") at the [University of Toronto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Toronto "University of Toronto") and Senior Investigator at the [Lunenfeld-Tanenbaum Research Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunenfeld-Tanenbaum_Research_Institute "Lunenfeld-Tanenbaum Research Institute"), [Sinai Health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinai_Health_System "Sinai Health System"), [Toronto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto "Toronto").

## Early life and education

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Daniel_J._Drucker&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Drucker was born and grew up in Montreal, went to high school in Ottawa, and then enrolled at the [University of Ottawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Ottawa "University of Ottawa"), studying science.[[9]](#cite_note-frs-9) In 1976, he moved to Toronto, where he studied medicine at the [University of Toronto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Toronto "University of Toronto"), graduating in 1980. He completed his internship at [Johns Hopkins Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johns_Hopkins_Hospital "Johns Hopkins Hospital") (1980–81) and completed his [internal medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internal_medicine "Internal medicine") and [endocrinology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endocrinology "Endocrinology") residencies at the [University of Toronto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Toronto "University of Toronto") (1981–84).[[9]](#cite_note-frs-9)

## Career and research

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Daniel_J._Drucker&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career and research")]

In 1984, Drucker began his research career at [Massachusetts General Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_General_Hospital "Massachusetts General Hospital") and [Harvard Medical School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Medical_School "Harvard Medical School"), studying molecular endocrinology in the lab of Professor [Joel Habener](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joel_Habener "Joel Habener") with the support from a Medical Research Council of Canada Centennial Fellowship. Drucker’s independent discoveries in Boston included the demonstration that [proglucagon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proglucagon "Proglucagon") could be cleaved into multiple [glucagon-like peptides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glucagon-like_peptide-1 "Glucagon-like peptide-1"), including several distinct isoforms of [GLP-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glucagon-like_peptide-1 "Glucagon-like peptide-1").[[10]](#cite_note-10) He then discovered that the truncated form of GLP-1(7-37) directly stimulated [cyclic AMP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyclic_AMP "Cyclic AMP") formation, [insulin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insulin "Insulin") secretion, and insulin [gene expression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gene_expression "Gene expression"); notably, it did so only when glucose levels were elevated.[[3]](#cite_note-:0-3)[[11]](#cite_note-11)

### Further discoveries of the therapeutic potential of GLP-1 at University of Toronto

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Daniel_J._Drucker&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Further discoveries of the therapeutic potential of GLP-1 at University of Toronto")]

In 1987 Drucker returned to Toronto, taking on the position of Assistant Professor of Medicine at the University of Toronto and continuing his research on the glucagon-like peptides while also working as a physician. In 1996, Drucker was one of several investigators who demonstrated that GLP-1 reduced food intake in preclinical studies. Notably, the experiments in the Drucker lab demonstrated that this action of GLP-1 in the brain required the functional canonical GLP-1 receptor.[[4]](#cite_note-:1-4) Drucker, together with colleagues at Tufts Universities, filed multiple patents describing the utility of targeting the [DPP-4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dipeptidyl_peptidase-4 "Dipeptidyl peptidase-4") enzyme, and published studies demonstrating that genetic or chemical inactivation of DPP-4 prevented degradation of GLP-1 and GIP, supporting the development of [DPP-4 inhibitors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dipeptidyl_peptidase-4_inhibitor "Dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitor") for the treatment of type 2 diabetes.[[12]](#cite_note-12)[[13]](#cite_note-13) In all, Drucker's discovery science has led to 33 issued US patents supporting translational drug development efforts in the field of peptide based therapeutics. Collectively, the body of work from multiple investigators and companies led to the development of two leading classes of [diabetes medications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diabetes_medication "Diabetes medication"): [GLP-1 receptor agonists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GLP-1_receptor_agonist "GLP-1 receptor agonist") and [DPP4 inhibitors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DPP4_inhibitors "DPP4 inhibitors").[[9]](#cite_note-frs-9)

### Discovery of GLP-2 actions leading to Short Bowel Syndrome treatments

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Daniel_J._Drucker&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Discovery of GLP-2 actions leading to Short Bowel Syndrome treatments")]

In 1996, Drucker also discovered the first biological actions for GLP-2, demonstrating that it augmented crypt cell proliferation and expansion of the mucosal epithelium in the [small bowel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Small_bowel "Small bowel") of mice and rats.[[14]](#cite_note-14) He subsequently identified and characterized a DPP-4-resistant molecule, teduglutide,[[15]](#cite_note-15) that was ultimately developed and approved for the treatment of [short bowel syndrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Short_bowel_syndrome "Short bowel syndrome") in adults and children, a disorder in which fluids are poorly absorbed after [resection of the small intestine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowel_resection "Bowel resection").[[9]](#cite_note-frs-9)[[16]](#cite_note-16)[[17]](#cite_note-17)

### Research supporting the development, safety and benefits of GLP-1 therapeutics

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Daniel_J._Drucker&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Research supporting the development, safety and benefits of GLP-1 therapeutics")]

Drucker joined the Samuel Lunenfeld Research Institute at Mount Sinai Hospital in Toronto in 2006. In 2008 he led studies aimed at the development and testing of the first long-acting, once-weekly version of the diabetes medication [exenatide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exenatide "Exenatide").[[18]](#cite_note-18) He later studied the long-term effects of related weight-loss medicines on bowel health.[[19]](#cite_note-19) Drucker has also led the identification of the cardioprotective mechanisms of GLP-1 action. Notably, in 2009 he demonstrated in mice that these effects were not dependent on glucose lowering or weight loss[[5]](#cite_note-:2-5) – findings confirmed over a decade later in cardiovascular outcome trials. His discoveries predicted the safety of GLP-1 receptor agonists for their expanding applications to treat obesity and other chronic conditions. Most recently, Drucker has identified multiple mechanisms linking GLP-1 to the reduction of inflammation[[6]](#cite_note-:3-6)[[20]](#cite_note-20).

Drucker holds the Banting and Best Diabetes Centre-Novo Nordisk Chair in [Incretin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incretin "Incretin") Biology. His many national and international recognitions include the 2023 [Wolf Prize in Medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolf_Prize_in_Medicine "Wolf Prize in Medicine"), awarded for "pioneering work in elucidating the mechanisms and therapeutic potential of enteroendocrine hormones," as well as the [Warren Alpert Foundation Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Alpert_Foundation_Prize "Warren Alpert Foundation Prize") and the [Canada Gairdner International Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_Gairdner_International_Award "Canada Gairdner International Award"), among numerous others. Drucker was elected a Royal Society Fellow in 2015, a National Academy of Sciences International Member in 2021and a National Academy of Medicine International Member in 2023. In 2024, he was named among *Time* magazine's 100 most influential people.

DANIEL J. DRUCKER

**Dr. Daniel J. Drucker** is University Professor in the Department of Medicine's Division of Endocrinology, University of Toronto; the Banting and Best Diabetes Centre-Novo Nordisk Chair in Incretin Biology; and a Senior Investigator at Sinai Health's [Lunenfeld-Tanenbaum Research Institute.](https://www.lunenfeld.ca/)

The Drucker Lab's studies of the physiology and molecular biology of the glucagon-like peptides have continuously advanced the science of peptide hormones and our understanding of their therapeutic potential. Dr. Drucker's foundational work has underpinned the development of two classes of medicine for type 2 diabetes (GLP-1 receptor agonists and DPP-4 inhibitors). He has also led the identification of the cardioprotective mechanisms of GLP-1 action, predicting the safety of GLP-1 receptor agonists for treatment of obesity and other chronic conditions. Most recently, the Drucker Lab has identified multiple mechanisms linking GLP-1 to the reduction of inflammation.
